hints: Look at the rod-shaped cells in Fig. 2.1 and recall the genus name you learned for the bacterium that infects the lungs to cause TB.
walkthrough:
Link the disease to its pathogen**
TB is a bacterial lung infection. The rod-shaped bacterium you see in the TEM is the classic TB bacterium, a Mycobacterium with a waxy cell wall.

Give the full binomial name**
The main human pathogen is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Write the genus with a capital M and the species in lower case, ideally in italics.
Final answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (accept Mycobacterium bovis).

hints: First decide if this immunity came from natural infection or from a medical intervention - was a vaccine given by injection?
walkthrough:
Artificial or natural?**
Natural means you meet the pathogen in everyday life. Here a BCG vaccine is made and given deliberately, so it is artificial.

Active or passive?**
Passive means you are given ready-made antibodies. Active means your own B and T lymphocytes respond to antigen and make your own antibodies and memory cells. BCG contains live non-pathogenic bacteria with antigens, so your body makes its own response. Together this is artificial active immunity.

hints: Rifampicin binds at a site other than the active site - think about what general type of enzyme inhibition this is and what it does to the whole enzyme shape.
Think about what RNA polymerase normally does with its active site during transcription - what must fit into it and what product is made?
Now link no mRNA to the next stage in protein synthesis - why would no mRNA mean no polypeptide at the ribosome?
walkthrough:
Non-competitive binding changes shape**
RNA polymerase is an enzyme, so its function depends on its precise 3D tertiary structure. When rifampicin binds away from the active site, it pulls the protein into a slightly different shape. That distortion is transmitted to the active site.

Active site no longer works in transcription**
Normally the active site is complementary to RNA nucleotides and joins them together on a DNA template to make mRNA. After distortion it is no longer complementary, so nucleotides cannot bind properly, the DNA cannot be transcribed and no mRNA is made.

No mRNA means no polypeptide**
Polypeptide synthesis happens by translation at ribosomes, and ribosomes need mRNA instructions to assemble amino acids in order. With no mRNA, translation is prevented and no new bacterial protein is made.

Final answer: Rifampicin is a non-competitive inhibitor that changes the tertiary structure / shape of the active site of RNA polymerase so it is no longer complementary to RNA nucleotides; RNA nucleotides are not joined so mRNA is not synthesised (no transcription) and translation cannot occur.

hints: Compare the first bar in 2009 with the last bar in 2013 - is the overall direction up, down or staying the same?
Now look year by year for where the bars hardly change and where they jump a lot - pick approximate values from the y-axis to support both points.
walkthrough:
State the overall trend**
From 2009 to 2013 the bars get taller overall. That is an overall increase in reported RR-TB and MDR-TB cases.

Support with numbers and detail**
Always quote figures with units. In 2009 there are about 52000 cases and by 2013 about 136000 cases. Then add the detail: between 2010 and 2011 there is very little change, about 66000 to 68000, whereas between 2011 and 2012 there is a large jump to about 110000, continuing up to 2013.

Final answer: Overall increase from 2009 to 2013, from approx. 52000 to approx. 136000 cases; very little change between 2010 and 2011 (approx. 66000 to 68000) but large increase between 2011 and 2012 / to 2013.

hints: Think about where variation comes from in bacteria before the drug is even used - what random change in DNA can alter a protein like RNA polymerase?
Think about what happens when rifampicin is present - which bacteria are killed and which survive to reproduce?
Think about how the surviving bacteria pass on their DNA - how does the resistance allele increase in frequency in the next generation?
Think about human behaviour that makes selection stronger - what happens if antibiotics are overused or the course is not finished?
walkthrough:
Mutation creates resistant variants**
In any large bacterial population, random mutations in DNA occur during replication. A few cells may by chance get a change in the gene for RNA polymerase so the protein has a different shape at the rifampicin binding site and rifampicin can no longer bind.

Antibiotic acts as a selection pressure**
When rifampicin is used, it kills sensitive bacteria but not the resistant mutants. This is natural selection - the resistant cells survive while the sensitive cells are selected against. Overuse for viral infections or over-prescribing, and stopping treatment early so a reservoir of bacteria remains, makes this selection stronger.

Resistant bacteria reproduce and spread the allele**
Survivors divide by binary fission and pass the resistance gene to offspring. This is vertical transmission. Resistance genes can also move between bacteria by horizontal gene transfer e.g. by plasmids.

Frequency of resistance increases**
Because only resistant bacteria contribute many offspring in the presence of the drug, the proportion of the population carrying the resistance allele rises over generations. That is how RR-TB and MDR-TB increase as seen in Fig. 2.2.

Final answer: Random mutation produces variation e.g. altered RNA polymerase binding site; antibiotic acts as selection pressure so sensitive bacteria are killed and resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; resistance allele is passed to offspring by vertical transmission and can spread by horizontal transmission, so frequency of resistance allele increases; overuse of antibiotics and not completing the course leaves a reservoir of bacteria for selection.
